messages.author: b6fd2925353976cd
messages.subject: installing Stan
parts:
Hi,

The manual says that the way to install Stan is:


To build Stan, first open a

command-line terminal application. Then change directories to the directory in which

Stan is installed (i.e., the directory containing the file named makefile).

% cd <stan-home>

Then make the library with the folloiwng make command.

% make bin/libstan.a


Here's the directory structure under stan-src-1.0.0 (below). There is no bin directory. In fact, there is no libstan.a anywhere under this directory.

ls
README.txt      lib             make            src
TO-DO.txt       licenses        makefile        web
doc             logos           rstan

What am I doing wrong here?

best,

Shravan

messages.author: bcfb6bc9f75aae0f
messages.subject: Re: installing Stan
parts:
Le dimanche 9 septembre 2012 10:57:48 UTC+2, Shravan Vasishth a écrit :
Hi,

The manual says that the way to install Stan is:


To build Stan, first open a

command-line terminal application. Then change directories to the directory in which

Stan is installed (i.e., the directory containing the file named makefile).

% cd <stan-home>

Then make the library with the folloiwng make command.

% make bin/libstan.a


Here's the directory structure under stan-src-1.0.0 (below). There is no bin directory. In fact, there is no libstan.a anywhere under this directory.

ls
README.txt      lib             make            src
TO-DO.txt       licenses        makefile        web
doc             logos           rstan

What am I doing wrong here?

Nothing.

Many programs use their arguments to specify their main input. E. g. "gcc foo.c" means "compile the C program foo.c" implicitly storing the relevant object file as foo.o).

"make" is different. Its main input is, by default,"makefile" in the current directory. If you open this file, you will see that this file defines targets and steps to obtain them. For example, one could have  makefile containing :

foo.o     foo.c
           gcc foo.c

makefile rules are intricate (see the man page for "make" to get a taste of it). In your case, "make bin/libstan.a" means "do whatever is necessary to build the target libstan.a in the bin directory, the steps being defined in the makefile". So type this exactly as written, and make will do its magic.

I'd recommend to take time to familiarize yourself with the Unix development environment, from where most of these tools come. They are command-line oriented, cryptic, as user-hostile as you can dream of, rather old by computer-science standards ... and frightfully powerful ! They became a de facto standard for development for good reasons...


HTH,

                                              Emmanuel Charpentier

best,

Shravan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: installing Stan
parts:
Shravan,

Before you get too frustrated, all you have to do is to first change
directory into the Stan directory, then type at the command line "make
bin/libstan.a". The static library will be built for you at
bin/libstan.a.

There really isn't a need to get familiar with make, we (the Stan dev
team) will try to encapsulate as much of the build pain through tools
such as make.



Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: installing Stan
parts:
On 9/9/12 3:38 PM, Shravan Vasishth wrote:
> Hi Daniel,
>
> yes, I did follow the instructions without thinking about it the second time round! Everything works as expected.
>
> Thanks, and apologies for the pointless thread.

Please don't feel it's your fault for not puzzling
out how to run Stan from the command line. This is our fault
for distributing software that doesn't install and
run like a regular desktop app. (RStan does run
like a regular R app.)

We're trying to make it as easy as possible
to use Stan, so this kind of question and feedback
is really useful to us. We'll work on making the usage
instructions clearer. Or ideally, figure out
how to get it run relocatably (any help on
the part of users who know how to do this better
than us would also be greatly appreciated).

In the meantime, please send us questions before
you get too frustrated. We're more than happy to
help.

- Bob
